in_text_mentions: Nevertheless, given the clinical context of chronic alcohol use and malnutrition, empirical supplementation with B-complex vitamins was promptly initiated. Lumbar puncture was unremarkable (5 leukocytes/mm³; glucose, 80 mg/dL; protein, 27 mg/dL; and lactate dehydrogenase, <30U/L). Electroencephalography showed diffuse slowing without epileptiform activity. Brain MRI demonstrated marked atrophy of the corpus callosum, particularly involving the body and splenium, with hypointensity on T1 and hyperintensity on T2-weighted images, consistent with subacute Marchiafava-Bignami syndrome (Figure 2).

A: Panel A shows T2-weighted MRI of the brain (7 days post-onset) revealing widespread hyperintense lesions in the corpus callosum, a finding associated with the acute phase of Marchiafava Bignami disease. B: Panel B shows post-gadolinium T1-weighted MRI (7 days post-onset) demonstrating enhancement in the splenium and extracallosal regions of the corpus callosum, consistent with acute inflammation in MBD. C: Panel C shows follow-up MRI (22 days post-onset) revealing necrotic changes without gadolinium enhancement in previously affected regions, indicating disease progression to necrosis in MBD.

Brain MRI demonstrated hyperintense lesions in the precentral gyrus bilaterally and in the splenium of the corpus callosum on FLAIR (Figure 1A). Laboratory test results included decreased vitamin B1 (14 ng/mL; normal: >24 ng/mL), and mild elevation of liver enzymes. The cerebrospinal fluid was normal.
